verses.note: The same God who is Elohim, creator of everything, is now called by his personal covenant name. The pairing tells the reader that the maker of the cosmos and the God who later bound himself to Israel are one and the same.

God names humanity as he named day, night, sky, land, and seas in chapter 1. Naming expresses his authority over what he has made, and human beings, for all their rule over the animals, receive their own name from him.

The verse joins two names: El Elyon, a title a Canaanite priest-king could use, and the LORD, the personal name of Abram's God. Abram does not reject the title; he claims it for the LORD, declaring that the Most High is not an unknown deity but the God who made promises to him.
Most divine names in Genesis are given by God or used in worship by the patriarchs. This one is given by an Egyptian slave out of her own encounter, and Scripture keeps it.
El Shaddai becomes the name of blessing and fruitfulness in Genesis (28:3, 35:11, 48:3, 49:25). The name is given here, at the point where only the power of God can make the promise come true.
El Olam joins El Elyon (Genesis 14:19), El Roi (16:13), and El Shaddai (17:1) among the names by which the patriarchs knew God, each drawn from an experience of him.

El was the common Semitic word for God and also the name of the high god in Canaanite religion. By naming the altar El Elohe Israel Jacob claims that El is no distant deity of the region but the God who met and renamed him.

El Shaddai is the name tied to the patriarchs' promises of offspring (17:1, 28:3, 48:3). Exodus 6:3 says God was known to the fathers by this name, which frames the patriarchal period as a time of promise awaiting the fuller self-revelation of the exodus.
El Shaddai in Genesis is the name of God attached to fruitfulness and promise. Invoking it here, Jacob appeals to God's own commitment to the family, not to his sons' cleverness.

El Shaddai is tied in Genesis to the promise of fruitfulness (17:1-2, 28:3, 35:11). Jacob's use of the name here, before adopting two boys, fits that pattern: the God who makes a barren family fruitful is the one he invokes.

Jacob gathers names for God in a single line: the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd (compare 48:15), and the Stone or Rock of Israel. Each names God by what he has been to Jacob: strength, care, and a sure foundation, possibly with a memory of the stone at Bethel (28:18-22).

God gives his name, but in a form that explains rather than labels him: he is the one who is, and the one who will be with his people. The name makes relationship possible without making God manageable.

The personal name joins God's being to his history with a family: YHWH is ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’. God is known not in the abstract but through what he has promised and done.

El Shaddai was the name tied to promises of offspring and land (Genesis 17:1; 28:3; 35:11). The name YHWH will now be tied to redemption, so that every later use of it recalls the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (20:2).
